title: Finding Rare Outcomes with pandas: An NFL Playoff Example
text:
I personally like finding rare events in datasets because they can make for interesting stories. They can also point to observations worth investigating, and that investigation can reveal a bigger picture in the data. A rare negative outcome might show us something to avoid, while a rare positive outcome can show us what went unusually well.
In this tutorial, we will use NFL data from 1999 through 2025 to search for teams that made the playoffs after a bad start. I expected fewer than 5% of teams that started 1-5 to recover. The actual rate was 2.9%, and one of those teams was the 2015 Kansas City Chiefs. After beginning 1-5, Kansas City won its final ten regular-season games and finished 11-5.
By the end, you will be able to use pandas to group outcomes, calculate event rates, and trace a rare result back to the observations that produced it.

title: Finding Rare Outcomes with pandas: An NFL Playoff Example
text:
Load and inspect the data
The dataset contains one row for each NFL team after each week of a season from 1999 through 2025. Each row shows the team’s record at that point and whether it eventually made the playoffs. We will start by importing pandas, reading the CSV file, and looking at the columns that matter most for this tutorial.
import pandas as pd

games = pd.read_csv("data/team_week_records.csv")

games[[
    "season", "team", "games_played", "record", "made_playoffs"
]].head()
Here is what those five columns represent:



Column
Meaning




season
The year the season began


team
The team’s abbreviation


games_played
The number of games the team had actually played


record
The team’s wins and losses at that point


made_playoffs
True if the team made the playoffs that season



We use games_played instead of the NFL week number because teams have bye weeks, meaning they get a week off and do not play a game. For example, a team in Week 7 may have played only six games. Using the number of games played lets us compare teams at the same point in their seasons.

title: Finding Rare Outcomes with pandas: An NFL Playoff Example
text:
Select the checkpoints
Instead of looking at every point in the season, we will compare records after 2, 4, 6, and 8 games. These checkpoints let us see how a poor start becomes harder to overcome as the season continues without making the analysis too long.
checkpoints = [2, 4, 6, 8]

checkpoint_games = games.loc[
    games["games_played"].isin(checkpoints)
].copy()

checkpoint_games = checkpoint_games.sort_values([
    "season", "team", "week"
])

checkpoint_games = checkpoint_games.drop_duplicates([
    "season", "team", "games_played"
])
The .isin() method keeps only rows where games_played matches one of our four checkpoints. We then sort the rows and use drop_duplicates() so that each team appears only once at each checkpoint in each season. This matters because a bye week can create another row for a team even though its number of games played has not changed. Including season prevents records from different years for the same team from being treated as duplicates.

title: Finding Rare Outcomes with pandas: An NFL Playoff Example
text:
Calculate playoff rates by record
Next, we group teams that had the same record at the same checkpoint. The groupby() columns define each group, while .agg() creates two new summaries. team_seasons counts how many teams had that record, and playoff_teams counts how many of them made the playoffs.
record_summary = checkpoint_games.groupby([
    "games_played", "wins", "losses", "ties", "record"
]).agg(
    team_seasons=("team", "count"),
    playoff_teams=("made_playoffs", "sum")
).reset_index()

record_summary["playoff_rate"] = (
    record_summary["playoff_teams"]
    / record_summary["team_seasons"]
)
This works because made_playoffs contains Boolean values: True is counted as 1 and False as 0 when the column is summed. A team in a different season counts as a separate observation, which is why we call the denominator team_seasons. The calculation is:
\[
\text{Playoff rate} = \frac{\text{playoff teams}}{\text{team-seasons with that record}}
\]
Finally, .reset_index() turns the grouping columns back into regular columns so we can filter and sort the results in the next step.

title: Finding Rare Outcomes with pandas: An NFL Playoff Example
text:
Find the rare playoff paths
Before searching for the worst starts, we keep only records where at least one team eventually made the playoffs. Without this filter, winless records such as 0-4, 0-6, and 0-8 would come first even though no teams recovered from them. Our goal is not just to find bad starts; it is to find unlikely recoveries.
successful_starts = record_summary.loc[
    record_summary["playoff_teams"] > 0
].copy()

rare_paths = (
    successful_starts
    .sort_values(
        ["games_played", "wins", "losses"],
        ascending=[True, True, False]
    )
    .groupby("games_played")
    .head(1)
)

rare_paths[[
    "games_played",
    "record",
    "team_seasons",
    "playoff_teams",
    "playoff_rate"
]]
The sort_values() step puts the fewest wins and most losses first within each checkpoint. We then group by games_played, and .head(1) keeps the first row in each group. Shown as percentages, the result is:

The six-game result stood out to me. Only 3 of the 102 teams that began 1-5 made the playoffs, giving a rate of 2.9%. That was even lower than my original guess of under 5%.

title: Finding Rare Outcomes with pandas: An NFL Playoff Example
text:
Investigate the 1-5 teams
Once we find a rare result, the next step is to return to the original observations and see which teams produced it. The conditions below select teams after six games, keep only 1-5 records, and require made_playoffs to be True. We also select the final wins and losses so we can compare how each season ended.
one_five_teams = checkpoint_games.loc[
    (checkpoint_games["games_played"] == 6)
    & (checkpoint_games["record"] == "1-5")
    & checkpoint_games["made_playoffs"],
    ["season", "team", "record", "final_wins", "final_losses"]
]

one_five_teams.sort_values("season")

Kansas City stands out because it won every remaining regular-season game. According to the Kansas City Chiefs’ account of the season, they became the first NFL team to start 1-5, finish on a ten-game winning streak, and make the playoffs.
To me, the timing makes the result even more interesting. Andy Reid had become the Chiefs’ head coach in 2013, and this comeback came one season before Kansas City began winning consecutive AFC West titles. Patrick Mahomes later became the full-time starting quarterback in 2018. Looking back, the 2015 season feels less like an isolated strange result and more like an early sign of the franchise’s future success.

title: Finding Rare Outcomes with pandas: An NFL Playoff Example
text:
Visualize the six-game checkpoint
A graph makes the 1-5 result easier to compare with the other records after six games. We first keep the six-game checkpoint and remove tied records from this graph to make the labels easier to read. The tied records were still included in the earlier analysis.
six_game_summary = record_summary.loc[
    (record_summary["games_played"] == 6)
    & (record_summary["ties"] == 0)
].sort_values("wins").copy()

six_game_summary["playoff_rate_percent"] = (
    six_game_summary["playoff_rate"] * 100
)

bar_colors = [
    "#E31837" if record == "1-5" else "#9AA0A6"
    for record in six_game_summary["record"]
]

playoff_chart = six_game_summary.plot.bar(
    x="record",
    y="playoff_rate_percent",
    color=bar_colors,
    legend=False
)

playoff_chart.set_title(
    "NFL Playoff Rate by Record After Six Games, 1999-2025"
)
playoff_chart.set_xlabel("Record after six games")
playoff_chart.set_ylabel("Teams that made the playoffs (%)")
The playoff rates are multiplied by 100 so the vertical axis displays percentages. The color list makes the 1-5 bar red and every other bar gray. Finally, pandas uses Matplotlib to create the bar chart and add the title and axis labels.



Playoff rates generally rise as a team’s six-game record improves, while the red 1-5 bar shows a 2.9% playoff rate.


The chart gives the rare event some context. Making the playoffs from 1-5 was possible, but teams in that position had very little room left for another loss.

title: Finding Rare Outcomes with pandas: An NFL Playoff Example
text:
What can you investigate next?
Using pandas, we turned weekly records into playoff rates, identified bad starts that still led to the playoffs, and traced a rare result back to the teams that produced it. The 1-5 result shows why finding a rare event is the start of an investigation, not the end. It led us to the bigger story of the 2015 Chiefs.
Next, replace made_playoffs with sb_champion in the aggregation and repeat the process. What is the worst start from which a team recovered to win the Super Bowl? You can also apply this method to another sport or any dataset with groups and a final outcome. Choose meaningful checkpoints, count the outcomes, calculate their rates, and investigate the rare observations you find.

title: Building an NFL Dataset for National Tight Ends Day
text:
National Tight Ends Day (NTED) takes place on the fourth Sunday in October. The eventual research question is: Do NFL tight ends perform better on NTED than on other Sundays, and is any difference specific to tight ends or also visible among wide receivers and running backs?
Answering that question requires more than one table. Weekly player statistics contain the performance measures, while the schedule supplies the actual date of each game. This post focuses on acquiring, joining, checking, and preparing those data. It includes only a small descriptive preview because a statistical comparison belongs in a later analysis.

title: Building an NFL Dataset for National Tight Ends Day
text:
National Tight Ends Day (NTED) takes place on the fourth Sunday in October. The eventual research question is: Do NFL tight ends perform better on NTED than on other Sundays, and is any difference specific to tight ends or also visible among wide receivers and running backs?
Answering that question requires more than one table. Weekly player statistics contain the performance measures, while the schedule supplies the actual date of each game. This post focuses on acquiring, joining, checking, and preparing those data. It includes only a small descriptive preview because a statistical comparison belongs in a later analysis.

title: Building an NFL Dataset for National Tight Ends Day
text:
Data source and scope
The data come from nflverse, a community project that maintains public NFL datasets. The Python package nflreadpy provides functions for downloading weekly player statistics and schedules. This project uses seven completed regular seasons, 2019 through 2025.
The two calls are short:
import nflreadpy as nfl

seasons = list(range(2019, 2026))
player_stats = nfl.load_player_stats(
    seasons, summary_level="week"
).to_pandas()
schedules = nfl.load_schedules(seasons).to_pandas()
The acquisition run on November 1, 2026 (November 2 in UTC) returned 129,812 player-stat rows and 1,960 schedule rows. The player table had 150 columns, and the schedule had 46. These totals include postseason records, which are removed later.
The original proposal reported a smaller feasibility check for 2025: 19,422 player-stat rows with 150 columns and 285 schedule rows with 46 columns. The new run reproduced all four of those values. This matters because the proposal values are no longer being treated as unverified current output.
The nflreadpy software is distributed under the MIT License. At the time of acquisition, the nflverse data repository identified these data under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. That license permits sharing with attribution, but the release page and license should be checked again before redistributing the cleaned file. nflverse must remain credited, and its data come without a warranty.

title: Building an NFL Dataset for National Tight Ends Day
text:
Combining player statistics with dates
The shared key is game_id. The schedule should contain exactly one row for each game, while the player table contains many rows for that game. That makes this a many-to-one join, not a many-to-many join.
Before merging, the code verifies that schedule game_id values are unique. Pandas then enforces the expected relationship:
joined = player_stats.merge(
    schedule_for_join,
    on="game_id",
    how="left",
    validate="many_to_one",
    indicator=True,
)
The indicator identifies any player row without a schedule match. The code also compares the season and week supplied by the two sources after the merge. These checks produced the following results:

All 129,812 player-stat rows matched one schedule row. This confirms the 2025 proposal result for the full seven-season acquisition rather than assuming that one season represented all years.

title: Building an NFL Dataset for National Tight Ends Day
section: Turning a holiday rule into data
text:
Turning a holiday rule into data
NTED is defined by a calendar rule rather than an NFL week number. The fourth Sunday can move between dates and weeks from year to year, so hard-coding one week would misclassify some games. The pipeline finds the first Sunday in October and adds 21 days:
from datetime import date

def fourth_sunday_in_october(year):
    first = date(year, 10, 1)
    days_until_sunday = (6 - first.weekday()) % 7
    return date(year, 10, 1 + days_until_sunday + 21)
Only a game played on that actual date receives is_nted = True. A separate is_sunday field makes it possible to compare NTED with other Sundays without accidentally including Thursday or Monday games.

title: Building an NFL Dataset for National Tight Ends Day
text:
Filtering and selecting useful fields
The joined data are restricted to records where both source tables identify the game as regular season. The position filter then keeps tight ends (TE), wide receivers (WR), and running backs (RB). The final file has 35,840 player-game rows and 34 columns:



Position
Player-game rows




TE
8,377


WR
16,859


RB
10,604



The retained columns fall into four groups:

identifiers and context: season, week, game ID, date, teams, player ID, player name, and position;
production: targets, receptions, receiving yards, receiving touchdowns, carries, rushing yards, and rushing touchdowns;
calendar features: Sunday and NTED flags, the season’s NTED week, and week relative to NTED;
constructed context: team targets, tight end targets, tight end target share, and player-season pregame baselines.

Keeping the game ID and date is important for auditing. Keeping both receiving and rushing measures also prevents the comparison among positions from focusing only on one kind of opportunity.

title: Building an NFL Dataset for National Tight Ends Day
text:
Building reproducible features

Team tight end target share
Team tight end target share is calculated as
\[
\text{TE target share} =
\frac{\text{targets to team tight ends}}
{\text{targets to all players on the team}}.
\]
This feature is created before filtering to TE, WR, and RB. As a result, the denominator includes every recorded target for the team, even if a target went to another position. If the denominator were zero, the share would be missing instead of being labeled zero. The acquired data had no team-game with a zero target denominator, but the rule remains in the code so a future run does not silently divide by zero.


Player-season baselines
Each row also includes the player’s average targets, receptions, receiving yards, receiving touchdowns, and carries in earlier appearances from that season. The current game is excluded. For example, a player’s baseline entering Week 8 uses only that player’s available Weeks 1–7 rows.
This choice prevents the outcome being compared from also changing its own baseline. A player’s first recorded appearance has no earlier evidence, so those baseline fields are intentionally missing. There are 3,634 such first-appearance rows. These are meaningful missing values and are not replaced by zero.


Other missing values
The source had no missing values in the seven retained box-score counting columns after the regular-season filter. The pipeline is still explicit: if a future player appearance row has a missing counting value, it records the number of replacements and fills that value with zero. It does not apply a blanket fill to dates, identifiers, shares, or baselines.

The main output is data/nted_player_games_2019_2025.parquet. Parquet preserves data types and stores the table in about 0.6 MB, making it more compact than a CSV version of the same records. The pipeline also writes data/nted_validation_2019_2025.json and data/nted_position_summary_2019_2025.csv. Those smaller files make the reported checks and preview table auditable without rerunning the download.
The complete workflow is in acquire_nted_data.py. From the project directory, it can be reproduced with:
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe acquire_nted_data.py
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m unittest discover -s tests -v
The code writes new NTED-specific filenames, so it does not overwrite the existing tutorial data or figure.

The tight end means do not all move in the same direction: targets are slightly lower on NTED, while receptions, receiving yards, and receiving touchdowns are slightly higher. Wide receivers also have higher means for several receiving measures on NTED, so the raw pattern is not obviously unique to tight ends. These small descriptive differences could reflect the mix of players, teams, and opponents rather than NTED itself.

title: Building an NFL Dataset for National Tight Ends Day
text:
Limits of this dataset
Only seven NTED dates are available, and bye weeks mean that not every team plays on each date. A weekly player-stat table also does not fully describe injuries, inactive players, snap counts, routes, or other differences in playing opportunity. Players who appear in the data may have very different roles, and missing appearances should not automatically be interpreted as zero performance.
Comparisons with nearby weeks can help identify whether an apparent change is isolated to NTED, while WR and RB comparisons provide useful context. Player-season baselines and team target share can also describe opportunity more carefully. Even with those additions, this observational dataset cannot establish that NTED causes performance to change.
This draft remains provisional until the complete assignment rubric is available.
